title: Chess, Blind Rage, and Education
author: Teach Students Not Classes
summary: The author argues that teachers who maintain at least one hobby they are genuinely bad at are better teachers, because the regular experience of failure, confusion, and the frustration of not yet understanding makes it impossible to dismiss student struggle with 'this lesson isn't that hard.' Using chess as his personal recurring frustration, the author traces how practicing competence can create a professional blindspot: when skills feel obvious, the teacher's explanations become abstract, the threshold for dismissing student errors rises, and the genuine cognitive and emotional experience of not-yet-knowing becomes inaccessible. The essay makes an argument for 'deliberate difficulty' — intentionally staying in the position of learner in something genuinely beyond one's current ability — as a professional discipline for educators. The key insight is that empathy in teaching is not primarily a dispositional quality but an epistemic one: you cannot genuinely understand student struggle if you have not recently experienced comparable struggle yourself. The piece is unconventional in teacher professional development literature and memorable for its honesty about how expertise erodes empathy.
points: The central professional development argument is unusual: being regularly bad at something outside your expertise is not a personal indulgence but a teaching-empathy practice, because it restores access to the experience of genuine confusion.

The 'this isn't that hard' rhetorical question is identified as a defense mechanism — it creates emotional distance from student non-understanding and implicitly attributes the learning failure to students rather than to instruction.

Expert blindspot is the cognitive underpinning: when a skill is automated, the conscious experience of acquiring it disappears, making it genuinely difficult for experts to reconstruct what learning it felt like — and therefore to scaffold it effectively.

The correlation between teacher frustration at their own hobbyist failures and classroom patience for student failure is the article's most testable claim: keeping that frustration alive appears to maintain the empathic responsiveness that expertise erodes.

The implication for teacher professional development is that some of the most important professional growth happens outside professional learning communities — in any context where the teacher is genuinely a struggling beginner.
quotes: Unable to stand the frustration of losing another game of chess, I slammed shut my laptop and summoned all of my self-control to keep from punching my desk. I wish I could say this was an isolated incident, but I have been in this situation dozens of times in my life.

Thinking, “This lesson is not that difficult, so there is no reason students should be confused,” creates emotional distance between the teacher and the learning—or lack of learning—happening in the classroom. If a lesson is not that difficult, then it must be the student’s fault for not understanding.

Veteran teachers will have taught some topics hundreds of times, and this level of subject consistency has many benefits. It allows us to use previously created materials and to fine-tune them throughout the years.

No matter how badly I want to be good at chess, I cannot seem to improve to a level I find satisfactory. Even when I do feel myself beginning to improve, this always seems to be followed by a demoralizing losing streak.

There have been times when I became so angry after a series of losses that I’ve had to force myself to give up chess for weeks at a time. Every week, they are forced to spend time wallowing in their aggravation.

Just because it is easy for us after the hundredth time does not mean it will be easy for our students on their first try. It is our job to be compassionate and patient and to find a way to reach our struggling students.
I admit that it hurt to hear these students didn’t understand the material. I could have let myself think, “Why are students still having trouble with this topic?
